overview: Version control is a system that records changes to your files over time, so you can see who changed what, when, and why - and roll back to any earlier version whenever you need to.

Git is the distributed version control tool that dominates software and data engineering: every copy of a project (every 'clone') contains the entire history, so you can work offline and there is no single point of failure.

The everyday model is simple: you edit files in your working directory, choose which changes to record (staging), then take a permanent, labelled snapshot called a commit - and the full chain of commits becomes the history you can navigate, share, and revert.
learningObjectives: Explain what version control is and why it exists, and describe how Git (distributed) differs from centralized systems like SVN or CVS.
Describe Git's core model: snapshots (not diffs), immutable commits identified by a SHA hash, and the three areas - working directory, staging area, and the .git repository.
Set up your identity, initialize or clone a repository, and record your first change with the edit -> stage -> commit lifecycle, then inspect history with git status and git log.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Version control (also called source control) is the practice of tracking and managing changes to a collection of files over time. A version control system (VCS) stores a complete, ordered history of those changes so that any past state can be reconstructed. Git is a distributed version control system (DVCS): rather than keeping the history on one central server, every clone holds the full repository - all files and their entire history. Git models history as a series of commits, where each commit is an immutable snapshot of the whole project at a moment in time, identified by a 40-character SHA-1 hash computed from its contents, and linked to its parent commit(s), plus metadata: author, committer, timestamp, and a message. Work flows through three areas: the working directory (the files you edit), the staging area (also called the index, where you assemble the next commit), and the repository (the .git directory, where commits are stored permanently). A special pointer called HEAD marks the commit you are currently working from.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine writing an important document and, instead of saving copies named report_final.docx, report_final_v2.docx, and report_final_REALLY_final.docx, you had a magic 'save point' button. Each time you press it you add a labelled photo of the entire project to a photo album, with a note saying what you changed and why. Version control is that album, and Git is the tool that manages it. Because you can flip back to any photo, you can undo a bad change instantly. The twist with Git is that everyone on the team carries their own complete copy of the album - not just the latest photo, but every photo ever taken. You can add photos while offline on a plane, and later merge your album with everyone else's. There are three places a change lives before it becomes a permanent photo: your desk where you are actually editing (the working directory), a tray where you place the pages you have decided to include (the staging area), and the album itself where the photo is finally glued in (the repository). Pressing 'save point' is called a commit.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Version control has a long lineage: SCCS (1972) and RCS (1982) tracked single files, then CVS (1990) and later Apache Subversion (SVN, 2000) introduced centralized systems where a single server held the authoritative history and developers checked files in and out over the network. Git was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds for the Linux kernel, after the kernel team lost free access to the proprietary BitKeeper tool. Torvalds wanted something fast, fully distributed, and cryptographically trustworthy - so Git gives every clone the entire history and identifies every commit by a SHA hash of its contents, making tampering detectable. Git's speed and distributed model, combined with the rise of hosting platforms like GitHub (2008), GitLab, and Bitbucket, made it the near-universal standard. Today it underpins not just application code but data engineering as a whole: SQL transformations, dbt models, Airflow DAGs, notebooks, and infrastructure-as-code all live in Git and drive automated CI/CD pipelines.

whyItMatters.business: Version control is the safety net for anything that runs the business: when a bad change breaks a revenue-reporting pipeline, Git lets the team see exactly what changed and roll back to a known-good version in minutes rather than reconstructing lost work, protecting deadlines, revenue, and trust in the data.
whyItMatters.engineering: Git is the shared source of truth that lets many engineers work on the same pipeline code, SQL models, and DAGs without overwriting each other, with every change reviewed, attributed, and reversible - turning collaboration from emailing zip files into a disciplined, auditable process.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because every clone is a full, independent copy of the history, hundreds of engineers across teams and time zones can work in parallel and later reconcile their work, and automated systems (CI/CD) can clone the exact same code to build, test, and deploy it consistently at any scale.
whyItMatters.cost: Reproducibility comes almost for free: any past state of a pipeline can be recreated exactly from its commit, so debugging a data issue, reproducing a report, or recovering from a mistake costs a checkout rather than hours of guesswork or re-derivation.
whyItMatters.reliability: Git makes changes reversible and traceable: a faulty transformation can be reverted to the previous commit, and the commit history plus messages tell you precisely what changed and why, so incidents are diagnosed and recovered from quickly instead of turning into outages.

coreComponents.name: Repository (.git directory)
coreComponents.definition: A repository is a project tracked by Git; the hidden .git directory at its root stores the entire history - every commit, snapshot, branch pointer, and configuration - as a content-addressed object database.
coreComponents.purpose: To hold the complete, permanent record of the project so any past version can be reconstructed and shared, independently of any server.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store all committed snapshots and their metadata, maintain branch and tag pointers and HEAD, and provide the object database that git commands read from and write to. Deleting .git turns a repo back into ordinary files with no history.
coreComponents.examples: git init (create a new repo) | git clone <url> (copy an existing repo, history and all) | the hidden .git/ folder | git status (reports state relative to the repo)

coreComponents.name: Working directory
coreComponents.definition: The working directory is the set of actual project files you see and edit on disk - the checked-out version of one commit, plus any changes you have made since.
coreComponents.purpose: To give you an ordinary, editable copy of the project to work on, which Git compares against the last commit to know what has changed.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Hold the current files you edit; be the place where changes originate before they are staged. Git classifies files here as untracked, modified, or unchanged relative to the commit that HEAD points to.
coreComponents.examples: editing pipeline.py in your editor | a new file model.sql that Git calls 'untracked' | git status showing 'modified' files | git diff (working directory vs staging)

coreComponents.name: Staging area (index)
coreComponents.definition: The staging area, also called the index, is an intermediate space where you assemble exactly the changes that will go into the next commit, using git add.
coreComponents.purpose: To let you craft a clean, focused commit by choosing which changes to include rather than committing everything at once.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Record the snapshot of files you have marked with git add so the next git commit captures precisely those, letting you group related changes and leave unrelated edits for a later commit.
coreComponents.examples: git add pipeline.py (stage one file) | git add . (stage everything) | git status showing 'Changes to be committed' | git diff --staged (staged vs last commit)

coreComponents.name: Commit (snapshot)
coreComponents.definition: A commit is a permanent, immutable snapshot of the staged project state, identified by a SHA hash and carrying a parent link, author, timestamp, and a human-written message.
coreComponents.purpose: To record a labelled point in history you can return to, understand, share, and revert - the fundamental unit of version control.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Capture the full project state at a moment, link to its parent to form the history chain, and store who made it, when, and why; its SHA is derived from its contents so any change produces a different commit.
coreComponents.examples: git commit -m "Add daily revenue transformation" | a SHA like 9f2a1c7 | git log (list commits) | git show 9f2a1c7 (inspect one commit)

internalWorking: When you initialize a repository with git init, Git creates a hidden .git directory containing an object database and pointers; from then on Git can compare the files on disk against what it has recorded and report exactly what has changed.

Git stores content as objects addressed by a SHA hash of their contents: a 'blob' holds the bytes of a file, a 'tree' lists the files and sub-trees in a directory (like a folder snapshot), and a 'commit' object points to one top-level tree plus its parent commit(s) and metadata. Identical content is stored only once because it hashes to the same address.

git add copies the current content of the chosen files into the staging area (the index), recording the blobs that will make up the next commit; this is why editing a file again after adding it means you must add it once more to capture the newer version.

git commit takes whatever is staged, writes a tree object describing that snapshot, creates a commit object that references the tree, the previous commit as its parent, and your identity and message, and computes a SHA over all of it - producing an immutable snapshot. Crucially Git records a full snapshot each time, not a diff; it simply reuses unchanged objects so snapshots stay compact.

HEAD is a pointer to the commit (usually via a branch) you are currently on; each new commit's parent is whatever HEAD pointed to, and then HEAD moves forward to the new commit. Because commits are chained by parent links and named by content hashes, the whole history is a tamper-evident graph - changing any old commit would change its hash and every commit after it.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Edit files in the working directory -> git add selects changes into the staging area (index) -> git commit writes a snapshot (tree + parent + author + message) into the .git repository and advances HEAD -> repeat to build a history chain -> git log / git show / git status to inspect -> git clone copies the whole repository (history included) to another machine
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You start a new pipeline project and run 'git init', which creates the hidden .git directory; Git now watches the folder but is tracking nothing yet. 'git status' reports your new files as 'untracked'.
2. You write revenue_pipeline.py and run 'git add revenue_pipeline.py'; Git copies that file's current content into the staging area, so 'git status' now lists it under 'Changes to be committed'.

3. You run 'git commit -m "Add initial revenue pipeline"'; Git writes a snapshot into the repository, stamps it with your name, email, and the time, computes a SHA (say 9f2a1c7), and moves HEAD to this first commit. This is now a permanent point you can return to.

4. You edit the file to add error handling, run 'git add revenue_pipeline.py' again to stage the newer version, and 'git commit -m "Handle missing input files"'; Git creates a second commit whose parent is the first, extending the history chain.

5. Later a change breaks the pipeline. You run 'git log --oneline' to see the two commits and their SHAs, 'git show 9f2a1c7' to inspect exactly what the first commit contained, and can check out that earlier snapshot to reproduce or roll back - all locally, with no server involved.

keyTerminology.meaning: A permanent, immutable snapshot of the staged project at a moment in time, identified by a SHA hash and carrying a parent link, author, timestamp, and message.
keyTerminology.importance: Commits are the unit of history: every save point, rollback, comparison, and code review is expressed in terms of commits, so understanding them is the foundation of using Git.

keyTerminology.meaning: A 40-character hexadecimal fingerprint (SHA-1) that Git computes from a commit's contents to name it; the same content always produces the same hash, and different content produces a different one.
keyTerminology.importance: The hash is how you refer to a specific version, and because each commit's hash depends on its contents and parent, the whole history is tamper-evident - you cannot quietly rewrite the past.

keyTerminology.meaning: The three places a change lives: the working directory is the files you edit, the staging area (index) is where you assemble the next commit with git add, and the repository (.git) is where committed snapshots are stored.
keyTerminology.importance: This three-area model explains what git add and git commit actually do, and why a change on disk is not saved to history until it is staged and then committed.

keyTerminology.meaning: A pointer to the commit you are currently working from - the parent of your next commit; it usually points at a branch, which in turn points at a commit.
keyTerminology.importance: HEAD tells Git (and you) 'where you are' in history; new commits build on it, and moving HEAD is how you check out different versions.

keyTerminology.meaning: A distributed system (Git) gives every clone the full history so work is local and offline-capable; a centralized system (SVN, CVS) keeps the authoritative history on one server that clients must reach for most operations.
keyTerminology.importance: This distinction explains Git's speed, offline capability, and resilience - and why 'git clone' downloads the entire history rather than just the latest files.

importantConcepts.explanation: A very common mental model is that Git saves the differences between versions - line X changed, line Y was added. That is how some older systems (like RCS/SVN internally) think, but Git is different: each commit is a full snapshot of every file at that moment. When a file has not changed between commits, Git does not copy it again; it simply reuses (points to) the existing stored object, because identical content hashes to the same address. So you get the mental simplicity of 'each commit is the whole project as it was then' with the storage efficiency of not duplicating unchanged files. This snapshot model is why checking out any commit gives you the entire project as it existed, and why operations like viewing an old version are fast and reliable - Git does not have to replay a long chain of diffs to reconstruct the past.

importantConcepts.concept: The three areas and the edit -> stage -> commit lifecycle
importantConcepts.explanation: Beginners often expect that editing a file 'saves' it to Git, but Git deliberately separates three steps. First you edit files in the working directory - ordinary changes on disk that Git sees as 'modified' or 'untracked'. Then you run 'git add' to move the specific changes you want into the staging area (the index), which is like a loading dock for the next commit. Finally 'git commit' takes exactly what is staged and writes it as a permanent snapshot in the repository. This staging step is a feature, not busywork: it lets you craft focused commits (for example, commit the SQL model fix in one commit and the unrelated typo fix in another) even though both changes sit in your working directory. Knowing which area a change is in - and that 'git status' tells you - removes almost all early confusion about why a change 'did not save'.

importantConcepts.concept: Git is distributed: every clone is a full backup
importantConcepts.explanation: In a centralized system like SVN, the real history lives on one server; if it is down you cannot commit, view history, or diff, and if it is lost without backups the history is gone. Git flips this: 'git clone' copies the entire repository - every file and every commit ever made - onto your machine. You can commit, branch, view the whole history, and diff completely offline, because everything you need is local; you only need the network to share with others (push/pull, covered in a later lesson). A powerful consequence is resilience: because every developer's clone contains the full history, there is no single point of failure - the project can be restored from any complete clone. This is exactly why Git feels fast (most operations touch only local data) and why it scaled to a project as large and distributed as the Linux kernel.

This trips up almost everyone at first. Git is the version control tool that runs on your machine and manages history locally - it was fully usable for years before GitHub existed. GitHub (and GitLab, Bitbucket, and self-hosted options) are hosting services that store a copy of your Git repository on the internet so teams can share it, review changes, and trigger automation. You can use Git with no account and no internet at all: init a repo, commit for months, and never touch a server. Conversely, GitHub adds collaboration features on top of Git - pull requests, issues, access control, CI/CD triggers - but the underlying versioning is still plain Git. Keeping the two separate in your head clarifies what 'git commit' (local) versus 'git push' (send to a remote host like GitHub) actually do, which we build on when we cover remotes.

variationsAndTypes: **Centralized VCS (CVS, Subversion/SVN):** a single server holds the authoritative history; clients check out files and must reach the server to commit or view history - simple to reason about but a single point of failure and awkward offline.

**Distributed VCS (Git, Mercurial):** every clone is a complete repository with full history, enabling offline work and no single point of failure; Git is by far the dominant DVCS in software and data engineering today.

**Git hosting platforms (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure Repos):** internet services that host a shared copy of a Git repo and layer on collaboration - pull requests, code review, issues, access control, and CI/CD - but the core versioning is still plain Git.

**Git object types (blob, tree, commit, tag):** blobs store file contents, trees describe directory structure, commits are snapshots with metadata and parent links, and annotated tags mark specific commits (like a release) - together they form Git's content-addressed model.

**Ways to start a repository (git init vs git clone):** git init turns an existing folder into a new empty repository, while git clone copies an existing remote repository - all files and full history - onto your machine to work on or contribute to.
advantages: **Full, navigable history:** every change is recorded with who, what, when, and why, so you can inspect, compare, and return to any past version of a pipeline or model.
**Reversibility and safety:** a bad change can be rolled back to a known-good commit, turning mistakes into a quick recovery rather than lost work or an outage.
**Collaboration without collisions:** many engineers can work on the same code and reconcile their changes through Git rather than emailing files or overwriting each other.
**Offline and resilient (distributed):** every clone holds the complete history, so you can work offline and the project survives the loss of any single machine or server.
**Reproducibility and automation:** any commit recreates an exact project state, and CI/CD systems clone that exact code to build, test, and deploy pipelines consistently.
disadvantages: **Learning curve:** the staging area, HEAD, and the distinction between local and remote confuse beginners, and Git's flexibility means many ways to get into a confusing state.
**Not built for large binary/data files:** Git tracks text changes efficiently but bloats when storing big datasets, model weights, or binaries - those need Git LFS or a separate data store.
**History can be rewritten:** commands that rewrite history are powerful but dangerous on shared branches, and can lose work or confuse collaborators if misused.
**Requires discipline:** the value depends on good, focused commits and clear messages; a repo full of vague 'update' commits gives little of Git's benefit.
**Not a secrets store:** committing credentials or private data leaves them in history even after deletion, so extra tooling and care are needed to avoid leaking sensitive information.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use Git for essentially all code and text-based configuration in data engineering: pipeline and application code, SQL transformations, dbt models, Airflow DAGs, notebooks, and infrastructure-as-code (Terraform), wherever you want history, collaboration, review, rollback, and reproducibility.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Do not use plain Git as a store for large datasets, model binaries, or high-volume changing data (use Git LFS, object storage, or a data-versioning tool instead), and never commit secrets or sensitive personal data; for those, use dedicated secret managers and data stores rather than the repository.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of writing a book with a magical, self-organizing photo album. Every time you finish a meaningful change, you take a photo of the entire manuscript and glue it into the album with a sticky note saying what you changed and why - that photo is a commit, and the note is the commit message. You never overwrite anything, so you can always flip back to any earlier photo (revert). Before each photo you lay only the pages you want to include onto a tray (the staging area) so the photo captures exactly the change you intend, not every half-finished scribble on your desk (the working directory). The clever part: instead of a single album on a shelf in one library (a centralized system), every co-author owns a complete copy of the album with every photo ever taken (Git is distributed). You can add photos on a plane with no internet, and later everyone reconciles their albums together. And crucially, the album (Git) is separate from the shared library building where you display a copy for others (GitHub) - you can keep your album at home and never visit the library at all.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Git and GitHub are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Git is the version control tool that runs locally on your machine and manages history; GitHub is a hosting service that stores a copy of a Git repo online and adds collaboration features (pull requests, issues, CI/CD). You can use Git with no internet and no GitHub account at all, and GitHub is just one of several hosts (GitLab, Bitbucket) built on top of plain Git.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Git stores the differences (diffs) between versions.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Git stores full snapshots. Each commit records the entire project as it was at that moment; unchanged files are not duplicated (Git reuses the existing stored object because identical content hashes the same), which gives snapshot simplicity with efficient storage. Git can compute diffs on demand for display, but the underlying storage is snapshots, not stored deltas.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need the internet or a central server to use Git.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Git is distributed: after 'git clone' (or a plain 'git init') you have the entire repository locally, so you can commit, view history, diff, and branch completely offline. You only need the network to share with others via push/pull to a remote - the core versioning happens entirely on your own machine.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Git scales to huge, distributed teams because most operations are local and every clone is self-contained; at very large scale teams add shallow/partial clones, monorepo tooling, and Git LFS for big files, and rely on hosting platforms to coordinate many contributors and automated pipelines.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Because every clone contains the full history and commits are content-hashed (tamper-evident), the repository is highly durable - it can be restored from any complete clone - but teams still back up the canonical remote and protect important branches from accidental force-pushes.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: The distributed model itself provides fault tolerance: there is no single point of failure, so the loss of the server or a developer's laptop does not lose history as long as one complete clone survives; production adds mirrored remotes and backups for the canonical copy.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: In data engineering, Git is monitored through the commit history and CI/CD: every change to pipeline code, SQL, or DAGs is attributed and reviewed, and automated checks (linting, tests, dbt runs) triggered on commits give visibility into what changed and whether it is safe.
productionConsiderations.security: Never commit secrets or sensitive data - they persist in history even after deletion; use secret managers, .gitignore, and pre-commit scanning, restrict who can push to protected branches, and rely on the hosting platform's access controls and signed commits for authenticity.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Reproducibility from commits reduces the cost of debugging and recovery, and keeping large data out of Git (using LFS or object storage) keeps repositories small, clones fast, and hosting costs low.
productionConsiderations.performance: Git's local-first design keeps everyday operations (commit, diff, log, status) near-instant; performance issues usually come from oversized binaries or bloated history, which are addressed by Git LFS, pruning, and shallow clones rather than by changing the workflow.

codeExamples.title: Set up your identity, create a repository, and make your first commit
codeExamples.overview: Configure who you are, turn a project folder into a Git repository, then record your first change with the edit -> stage -> commit lifecycle and inspect it.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) One-time setup: tell Git who you are (stamped onto every commit)
git config --global user.name "Ada Engineer"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"

# 2) Verify your configuration
git config --list

# 3) Turn the current folder into a new, empty Git repository
cd ~/projects/revenue-pipeline
git init

# 4) Create a file, then see what Git thinks of it (it is untracked)
echo "print('hello pipeline')" > pipeline.py
git status

# 5) Stage the file (move the change into the staging area)
git add pipeline.py

# 6) Record a permanent snapshot with a clear message
git commit -m "Add initial pipeline script"

# 7) View the history you just created
git log --oneline
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git config --global user.name/user.email' set your identity once for all repos; Git stamps this onto every commit as the author. 'git config --list' shows the effective settings. 'git init' creates the hidden .git directory, turning the folder into a repository. After creating pipeline.py, 'git status' reports it as 'Untracked' because Git is not yet recording it. 'git add pipeline.py' stages it (moves the change into the index for the next commit). 'git commit -m' writes the snapshot with your message and computes its SHA. 'git log --oneline' lists commits one per line with their short SHA and message.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/ada/projects/revenue-pipeline/.git/

$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	pipeline.py

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

$ git commit -m "Add initial pipeline script"
[main (root-commit) 9f2a1c7] Add initial pipeline script
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 pipeline.py

$ git log --oneline
9f2a1c7 Add initial pipeline script
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting 'git config' means Git may refuse to commit or stamp commits with a wrong/placeholder identity. Running git commands outside a repository gives 'fatal: not a git repository' - run 'git init' or 'cd' into a cloned repo first. Editing a file after 'git add' but before committing captures the older staged version; run 'git add' again to include the latest changes.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Set a default branch name and editor once with 'git config --global init.defaultBranch main' and 'git config --global core.editor "code --wait"'. Use 'git status -s' for a compact status, and 'git add -p' to stage changes hunk-by-hunk so each commit stays focused.

codeExamples.title: Clone an existing repository and explore its history
codeExamples.overview: Copy an existing project - all files and its entire history - onto your machine, then inspect the commit graph to understand how it evolved.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) Clone a repository (downloads every file AND the full history)
git clone https://github.com/example-org/data-pipelines.git

# 2) Move into the cloned project
cd data-pipelines

# 3) Confirm it is a repo and see the current state
git status

# 4) List recent commits compactly, with branches drawn as a graph
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -10

# 5) See who last changed each line of a file (great for context)
git blame dags/daily_load.py

# 6) Inspect one specific commit in full (changes + metadata)
git show 4c1d9ab
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git clone <url>' copies the remote repository in full - all files plus the complete commit history - so after cloning you can work entirely offline. 'cd' enters the project. 'git status' confirms a clean working tree on the default branch. 'git log --oneline --graph --decorate -10' shows the last 10 commits as a compact graph with branch/tag labels, revealing how history branched and merged. 'git blame' annotates each line of a file with the commit and author that last touched it. 'git show <sha>' prints one commit's metadata and the exact changes it introduced.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ git clone https://github.com/example-org/data-pipelines.git
Cloning into 'data-pipelines'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 1284, done.
remote: Total 1284 (delta 0), reused 1284 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
Receiving objects: 100% (1284/1284), 3.42 MiB | 6.10 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (612/612), done.

$ git log --oneline --graph --decorate -10
* 4c1d9ab (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Fix null handling in daily_load DAG
* a7e330f Add dbt model for revenue by region
* 1b90c42 Bump Airflow to 2.9 and adjust imports
* 82f5d1e Initial pipeline scaffolding
codeExamples.commonIssues: Cloning over HTTPS without credentials fails for private repos ('Authentication failed') - use a token or SSH key. Running commands before 'cd' into the cloned folder gives 'not a git repository'. A very large repo clone can be slow or huge because of big binary files in history; a shallow clone ('--depth 1') fetches only recent history when you do not need it all.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use 'git clone --depth 1 <url>' for a fast, shallow clone when you only need the latest code. Alias 'git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all' (e.g. as 'git lg') to visualize all branches at once. 'git show --stat <sha>' summarizes which files a commit changed without printing full diffs.

codeExamples.title: Minimal end-to-end: init, build a pipeline file, commit twice, and inspect
codeExamples.overview: Walk through the full local lifecycle on a tiny data pipeline: initialize a repo, make two focused commits, view the history, and show exactly what a commit changed.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) Create and initialize a fresh repository
mkdir daily-etl && cd daily-etl
git init

# 2) Add a .gitignore so we never commit noise or secrets
printf "__pycache__/\n*.pyc\n.env\n" > .gitignore

# 3) Create the first version of the pipeline
cat > etl.py <<'PY'
def run():
    print("loading data")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()
PY

# 4) Stage everything and make the first commit
git add .
git commit -m "Add initial ETL script and .gitignore"

# 5) Improve the script, then stage and commit just that change
sed -i 's/loading data/loading data for 2026-07-02/' etl.py
git add etl.py
git commit -m "Log the processing date in ETL run"

# 6) Review the history and inspect the latest change
git log --oneline
git show HEAD
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git init' starts the repo. Writing a '.gitignore' tells Git to ignore caches and secret files like .env so they never get committed. 'cat > etl.py' creates the first pipeline. 'git add .' stages all new files and 'git commit -m' records the first snapshot. Editing the file with 'sed', then 'git add etl.py' and a second 'git commit', creates a second, focused commit whose parent is the first. 'git log --oneline' shows both commits and their SHAs; 'git show HEAD' displays the most recent commit's metadata and its exact diff (the single changed line).
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ git commit -m "Add initial ETL script and .gitignore"
[main (root-commit) 3e5b8a2] Add initial ETL script and .gitignore
 2 files changed, 6 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 etl.py

$ git log --oneline
7c40de1 Log the processing date in ETL run
3e5b8a2 Add initial ETL script and .gitignore

$ git show HEAD
commit 7c40de1f9b2c4a6d8e0f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d
Author: Ada Engineer <ada@example.com>
Date:   Thu Jul 2 10:14:33 2026 +0000

    Log the processing date in ETL run

codeExamples.commonIssues: Committing without a .gitignore often pulls in __pycache__, virtualenvs, or a .env full of credentials - add .gitignore first. 'git add .' can stage more than intended; check 'git status' before committing. Writing vague messages like 'update' makes history useless; each commit message should say what changed and why.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep commits small and focused so 'git log' and 'git show' tell a clear story and rollbacks are surgical. Use 'git commit -v' to see the full diff while writing the message. Adopt a message convention (e.g. 'feat:', 'fix:') so history is scannable and can drive automated changelogs.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A data team's daily revenue pipeline suddenly starts producing wrong numbers after a recent change, and leadership needs the correct dashboard restored quickly while the team figures out what broke - all without losing anyone's in-progress work.
endToEndExample.inputData: A Git repository containing the pipeline code, SQL transformations, and an Airflow DAG, with a history of commits (each a snapshot with author, timestamp, and message) recording every change made to the pipeline over the past weeks.
endToEndExample.architecture: The project lives in Git: engineers edit files in their working directories, stage focused changes with git add, and record them as commits in the local .git repository, which mirrors a shared hosted remote. History is a chain of immutable, SHA-identified commits, so any past known-good state can be identified with git log and reconstructed exactly, and a bad change can be reverted commit-by-commit.
processingSteps: 1. Reproduce the state: run 'git log --oneline --graph -20' to list recent commits and read the messages, identifying which change likely introduced the wrong numbers.
2. Confirm the culprit: run 'git show <suspect-sha>' to see exactly what that commit changed - here, a modified SQL join that dropped rows - matching the symptom.
3. Verify against a known-good version: 'git log' points to the commit before the bad change; 'git show <good-sha>' confirms the previous, correct join logic.

4. Restore quickly: create a fresh commit that reverts the faulty change (undoing exactly that commit's diff) so the pipeline returns to correct output while preserving full history and everyone's other work.
5. Communicate and review: the revert commit's message references the incident and the reverted SHA; teammates see attribution and reasoning in 'git log', and the fix goes through normal code review.

6. Prevent recurrence: because every change is attributed and reproducible, the team adds a test around the join and relies on CI triggered from Git to catch a similar regression before it reaches production.
endToEndExample.output: A restored, correct revenue dashboard within minutes, plus a clean audit trail: the history shows the faulty commit, the revert that fixed it, who did what, and why - with no work lost.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The commit history itself is the audit log - git log and git show reveal exactly what changed, when, by whom, and why - and CI/CD checks triggered on each commit provide ongoing signal about whether new changes are safe.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Because commits are immutable snapshots, the fix is a forward-moving revert commit rather than an in-place edit of history, so the correction is itself recorded and reviewable; if the revert were wrong, it too could be reverted, and no prior work is destroyed.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The incident is resolved fast and safely: version control let the team pinpoint the exact change, roll back reliably, keep everyone's work intact, and leave a transparent record - illustrating precisely why Git underpins reproducible, collaborative, and recoverable data engineering.

industryUseCases.company: Analytics engineering teams versioning dbt and SQL models
industryUseCases.problem: SQL transformations and dbt models were edited directly in a warehouse or shared drive, so there was no record of who changed a metric definition or how to undo a change that skewed a report.
industryUseCases.solution: Keep all dbt models and SQL in a Git repository: every change is a reviewed commit with a message, history shows how a metric evolved, and a bad change is reverted to a known-good commit.
industryUseCases.benefits: Full attribution and history for metric definitions, safe rollback of faulty transformations, and reproducible reports because any commit recreates the exact model that produced a number.

industryUseCases.company: Platform teams managing Airflow DAGs and pipeline code
industryUseCases.problem: Pipeline code and DAGs were copied onto servers by hand, making it impossible to know what version was actually running or to roll back a deployment that broke jobs.
industryUseCases.solution: Store all DAGs and pipeline code in Git; deployments clone or check out a specific commit, so the running version is always known and CI/CD triggered from Git tests and deploys it.
industryUseCases.benefits: A single source of truth for what is deployed, reliable rollback by redeploying a previous commit, and consistent, automated deployments across environments.

industryUseCases.company: DevOps/Infrastructure teams doing GitOps with Terraform
industryUseCases.problem: Cloud infrastructure was changed manually in consoles, causing drift, undocumented changes, and no easy way to revert a misconfiguration that caused an outage.
industryUseCases.solution: Define infrastructure as code (Terraform) stored in Git, where every change is a commit and merges trigger automated plan/apply; the repository is the declarative source of truth.
industryUseCases.benefits: Auditable, reviewable infrastructure changes, easy rollback to a previous committed configuration, and reproducible environments built from a known commit.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Git scales to thousands of contributors because everyday operations are local and each clone is self-contained; at scale teams use hosting platforms to coordinate merges and reviews, shallow or partial clones to avoid pulling huge histories, monorepo tooling for very large codebases, and Git LFS to keep large binaries out of the main object database.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: The distributed model is inherently fault tolerant: since every clone holds the entire history, no single machine is a point of failure, and the repository can be reconstructed from any complete copy; teams still mirror the canonical remote and back it up so the authoritative copy is protected.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Hosting platforms run the shared remote in a highly available configuration with replicas and failover, while developers can keep working locally even if the remote is briefly unreachable, because commits, diffs, and history are all local operations.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Recovery is straightforward: because content-addressed commits make history tamper-evident and every clone is a full backup, a lost server can be restored from any developer's clone or a mirror; regular backups of the canonical remote and protected branches guard against accidental deletion or force-push.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep repositories fast by keeping them small: exclude build artifacts and data via .gitignore, move large files to Git LFS or object storage, prune stale branches, and use shallow/partial clones in CI where full history is not needed; most slowness comes from bloated history, not from Git itself.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Reproducibility from any commit cuts debugging and recovery costs, and keeping large data out of Git keeps clone times and hosting storage low; automating build/test/deploy from Git (CI/CD) avoids costly manual, error-prone releases.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Never commit secrets or sensitive data - they remain in history even after deletion, so use .gitignore, pre-commit secret scanning, and rotate any leaked credential; protect important branches, require reviews, use signed commits for authenticity, and rely on the platform's access controls and audit logs.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: In data engineering, Git is the observability layer for change: commit history and messages record what changed and why, CI/CD status shows whether each change passed tests and deployed, and blame/log let you trace any line of code, SQL, or DAG back to the change and reasoning that produced it.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Versioning transformations and pipeline code in Git enables reproducibility and testing: tests and data-quality checks run automatically on each commit through CI, and because any commit recreates an exact pipeline state, a suspicious result can be reproduced and validated against the version that produced it.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: The commit log itself is a durable, attributed record of every change; combined with CI/CD notifications (build failures, failed tests, blocked merges) and platform audit logs, teams are alerted to risky or failing changes before they reach production and can trace incidents to specific commits afterward.

recommendedPractices: **Commit early, often, and small:** make each commit one focused, working change so history is readable and rollbacks are surgical rather than all-or-nothing.
**Write clear commit messages:** state what changed and why (a concise summary line plus context), because the message is what your future self and teammates rely on.
**Use .gitignore from the start:** exclude caches, build artifacts, virtualenvs, large data, and secret files (.env) so the repo stays clean and safe.
**Set your identity once:** configure 'user.name' and 'user.email' globally so every commit is correctly attributed.
**Inspect before you commit:** run 'git status' and 'git diff' to confirm exactly what you are staging, avoiding accidental or unrelated changes.
engineeringStandards: Keep everything text-based that defines the pipeline - code, SQL, dbt models, DAGs, and infrastructure-as-code - under version control as the single source of truth.
Never commit secrets, credentials, or sensitive personal data; use secret managers and .gitignore, and treat any accidental leak as a rotate-the-credential incident.
Keep large binaries and datasets out of plain Git; use Git LFS or external object storage so clones stay fast and history stays small.
designRecommendations: Structure a repository so related pipeline code, SQL, and configuration live together, making changes reviewable and reproducible as a unit.
Treat the repository as the deployable source of truth: what runs in production should correspond to a specific committed version, not a hand-edited server file.
Distinguish local operations (init, add, commit) from sharing operations (push/pull to a remote) in your mental model so the workflow stays clear as you scale up.
namingConventions: Name repositories descriptively after the project or domain (e.g. revenue-pipeline, marketing-dbt) so their purpose is obvious.
Write commit summary lines in the imperative mood ('Add revenue model', 'Fix null handling') for consistency and readability in git log.
Adopt an optional prefix convention for messages (feat:, fix:, chore:) so history is scannable and can drive automated changelogs.
documentationStandards: Keep a README in the repository explaining what the project is, how to set it up, and how to run and test the pipeline.
Let commit messages document the 'why' behind changes so history serves as a decision log, not just a list of edits.
Document the branching and contribution workflow (even briefly) so new team members know how to make and submit changes.
testingStrategies: Run automated tests and linters on each commit via CI so regressions in pipeline code or SQL are caught before merging.
Verify reproducibility by checking out a past commit and confirming it recreates the expected pipeline state and outputs.
Test the rollback path: practice reverting a change to a known-good commit so recovery is fast and familiar during a real incident.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing secrets, large data, or generated files into the repository.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: A quick 'git add .' scoops up everything in the folder, including a .env file, a big dataset, or a __pycache__ directory, and beginners do not realize history is permanent.
commonMistakes.impact: Secrets remain retrievable in history even after being deleted (a security incident), and large or generated files bloat the repo, slowing clones for everyone.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Create a .gitignore before your first commit to exclude secrets, data, and artifacts, review 'git status' before committing, and use Git LFS or external storage for large files.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing vague, meaningless commit messages like 'update' or 'fix stuff'.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Committing feels like a chore, so people rush the message, not realizing it is the primary way history communicates intent later.
commonMistakes.impact: The history becomes useless for understanding what changed and why, making debugging, code review, and rollback far slower during an incident.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Write a concise imperative summary of what changed plus, when useful, a short body explaining why; keep commits focused so one message describes one coherent change.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a change is 'saved' in Git just because the file was edited and saved on disk.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The three-area model (working directory, staging, repository) is non-obvious, and other tools auto-save, so people expect Git to as well.
commonMistakes.impact: Work is not actually recorded in history, so it cannot be recovered, shared, or rolled back; a crash or checkout can lose unsaved-to-Git edits.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Learn the edit -> stage (git add) -> commit (git commit) lifecycle, use 'git status' to see which area a change is in, and commit when a change is meaningful and complete.

comparisonSection.explanation: Git gives every clone the complete history, so you can commit, diff, branch, and view history offline, and there is no single point of failure - any full clone can restore the project. Centralized systems keep the authoritative history on one server that clients must reach for most operations, which is simpler to reason about but fragile: server downtime blocks work and server loss without backups loses history. Git's model is why it feels fast and scaled to huge distributed projects.

Git records each commit as a full snapshot of the project, reusing unchanged file objects so it stays compact - checking out any commit reconstructs the whole project instantly without replaying a chain of changes. Delta-based systems store the differences between versions, which can be storage-efficient for small text edits but slower to reconstruct an old version and more fragile if any delta in the chain is corrupted. Git computes diffs for display on demand but stores snapshots underneath.

Git is the program on your machine that manages history - init, add, commit, log all work with no internet. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket are services that host a shared copy of a Git repo online and add collaboration features (pull requests, issues, access control, CI/CD). You can use Git entirely without any of them; conversely those platforms build on top of plain Git rather than replacing it. Conflating the two causes confusion about what 'commit' (local) versus 'push' (send to a host) do.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is version control, and why do teams use it?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Version control is a system that records changes to files over time so you can see who changed what, when, and why, and return to any earlier version. Teams use it to collaborate on the same code without overwriting each other, to review changes, to roll back mistakes safely, and to reproduce any past state - replacing error-prone habits like emailing zip files or keeping files named final_v2_FINAL.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the core idea (tracked history + revert) and the practical benefits (collaboration, rollback, reproducibility). Mentioning the 'final_v2' anti-pattern shows you understand the problem it solves.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Git is the version control tool that runs locally on your machine and manages history - you can init a repo, commit, and view history with no internet. GitHub is a hosting service that stores a copy of a Git repository online and adds collaboration features like pull requests, issues, access control, and CI/CD. GitLab and Bitbucket are alternative hosts. Git is the tool; GitHub is one place to host what Git produces.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This is a classic clarity check. The key point is that Git is local and standalone while GitHub is an optional online host built on top of it; naming alternatives (GitLab, Bitbucket) reinforces the distinction.

intermediateQuestions.question: Explain the three areas in Git and the lifecycle of a change.
intermediateQuestions.answer: Git has the working directory (the files you edit on disk), the staging area or index (where you assemble the next commit with git add), and the repository (.git, where committed snapshots are stored). A change flows edit -> stage -> commit: you modify files in the working directory, run 'git add' to stage exactly the changes you want, then 'git commit' to record them as a permanent snapshot. 'git status' tells you which area each change is in, and staging lets you craft focused commits.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The interviewer is checking that you understand why 'git add' exists and what commit actually captures. Emphasizing that staging lets you build focused commits shows real understanding, not memorization.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does a distributed VCS like Git differ from a centralized one like SVN?
intermediateQuestions.answer: In a centralized system (SVN, CVS) the authoritative history lives on one server, and clients must reach it to commit or view history, so the server is a single point of failure and offline work is limited. In Git, 'git clone' copies the entire repository - all files and full history - to your machine, so you can commit, diff, branch, and browse history offline, and any complete clone can restore the project. You only need the network to share via push/pull.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Look for the two consequences interviewers care about: offline capability and no single point of failure. Noting that clone downloads full history (not just latest files) shows you understand what 'distributed' actually means.

advancedQuestions.question: Does Git store diffs or snapshots, and what is a commit made of?
advancedQuestions.answer: Git stores snapshots, not diffs. Each commit is a full snapshot: a commit object points to a top-level tree (which describes the directory structure via blobs for file contents and sub-trees), plus its parent commit(s), author/committer, timestamp, and message. The commit is named by a SHA hash computed over its contents. Unchanged files are not duplicated - Git reuses the existing object because identical content hashes the same - so snapshots stay compact. Git computes diffs on demand for display.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This tests deeper understanding of Git's object model. Strong answers name blob/tree/commit objects, content-addressing by SHA, and the parent link, and clarify that diffs are computed, not stored.

advancedQuestions.question: Why is Git's history considered tamper-evident, and what does HEAD point to?
advancedQuestions.answer: Each commit's SHA is computed from its contents, including its parent's hash, so the commits form a hash chain: altering any past commit changes its hash and every commit after it, making tampering detectable. HEAD is a pointer to the commit you are currently on - usually indirectly, by pointing at a branch that points at a commit; your next commit's parent is whatever HEAD references, and HEAD then advances to the new commit. This is how Git tracks 'where you are' and builds the history chain.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the link between content-addressing and integrity, plus a correct mental model of HEAD as a moving pointer (typically via a branch) that determines each commit's parent.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A teammate deployed a change to a shared SQL transformation this morning and now a key dashboard shows wrong numbers. Leadership wants it fixed fast without losing other in-progress work. How do you use Git to handle this?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: First understand what changed by reading recent history rather than guessing. Use git log to list recent commits and messages, then git show on the suspect commit to confirm it altered the transformation in a way that matches the symptom. Confirm the previous version was correct. Then restore correct output in a way that preserves history and everyone else's work - a forward revert commit rather than destructive history editing. Finally leave a clear trail and add a safeguard so it does not recur.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Run 'git log --oneline --graph -20' to find the suspect commit and read messages, then 'git show <sha>' to confirm exactly what it changed and that it matches the bad numbers. Verify the prior commit had correct logic with 'git show <good-sha>'. Create a revert commit that undoes that specific change so the pipeline returns to correct output while keeping full history and all other work intact, with a message referencing the incident and reverted SHA. Put the fix through normal review, then add a test around the transformation and rely on CI to catch a similar regression next time.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design how a data engineering team should manage all of its pipeline code, SQL/dbt models, Airflow DAGs, and infrastructure-as-code so that changes are reviewable, reproducible, safely reversible, and drive automated deployment.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Put everything text-based (code, SQL, dbt models, DAGs, Terraform) in Git repositories as the single source of truth. Engineers work locally (edit -> stage -> commit), then share via a hosted remote (GitHub/GitLab) where changes are reviewed before merging. Configure .gitignore to exclude secrets, data, and artifacts; keep large files in Git LFS or object storage. Trigger CI/CD from the remote to lint, test, and deploy the exact committed version, so what runs in production always maps to a specific commit and can be rolled back by redeploying a previous one.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Git plus a hosting platform adds process (reviews, CI setup) and a learning curve, but delivers attribution, reproducibility, rollback, and automation that manual file management cannot. Plain Git is poor for large binaries and secrets, so those need LFS/object storage and secret managers respectively. Requiring reviews and CI slows individual changes slightly in exchange for far fewer production incidents.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: As the team and codebase grow, use protected branches and required reviews, split or organize repos (or adopt monorepo tooling) to keep them navigable, use shallow/partial clones in CI, offload large artifacts to LFS/object storage, and rely on the highly available hosted remote plus every clone being a full backup for resilience - while checkpointing production state to specific commits so any scale-out or recovery reproduces a known-good version.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Version control tracks changes to files over time so you can see who changed what and revert; Git is the distributed tool where every clone holds the full history and you record labelled snapshots (commits) via edit -> stage (git add) -> commit.
keyConcepts: A commit is an immutable snapshot identified by a SHA hash, with a parent link, author, timestamp, and message.
Three areas: working directory (edit) -> staging area/index (git add) -> repository/.git (git commit).
Git stores snapshots, not diffs, reusing unchanged file objects so storage stays compact.
Git is distributed: every clone has the full history, so you can work offline with no single point of failure.
Git is the local tool; GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket are optional hosting services built on top of it.
commands: git config --global user.name "Ada"   # set your identity for all commits
git init                                # turn the current folder into a new repo
git clone <url>                         # copy an existing repo with full history
git add pipeline.py                     # stage a change for the next commit
git commit -m "message"                 # record a snapshot with a message
git log --oneline --graph               # view compact, graphical history
interviewPoints: Version control = tracked, revertible history; Git is the distributed tool that does it.
A commit is an immutable, SHA-named snapshot with a parent, author, and message - snapshots, not diffs.
Three areas and the edit -> add -> commit lifecycle; 'git status' shows where a change is.
Distributed means every clone is a full copy: offline work and no single point of failure.
Git is not GitHub - Git is local; GitHub is an optional host with collaboration features.
quickNotes: Add a .gitignore before your first commit to keep out secrets, data, and artifacts.
Editing a file after 'git add' means you must add it again to capture the newer version.
HEAD points to the commit you are on and becomes the parent of your next commit.
Secrets stay in history even after deletion - rotate the credential if one is committed.
Keep commits small and messages clear so history is useful for debugging and rollback.

keyTakeaways: Version control records changes to files over time - who changed what, when, and why - so you can compare versions and revert safely, replacing brittle habits like final_v2_FINAL files and emailing zips.

Git is a distributed version control system: 'git clone' (or 'git init') gives you the entire repository and history locally, so you can commit, diff, and browse offline, and no single machine is a point of failure - unlike centralized systems such as SVN or CVS.

A commit is an immutable snapshot of the whole project (not a stored diff), named by a SHA hash and linked to its parent with an author, timestamp, and message; unchanged files are reused, so history is both simple to reason about and compact.

Changes flow through three areas - working directory (edit), staging area/index (git add), and repository/.git (git commit) - and 'git status' shows where each change is, which is the key to removing early Git confusion.

In data engineering, versioning pipeline code, SQL, dbt models, DAGs, and infrastructure-as-code in Git delivers reproducibility, collaboration, code review, reliable rollback of bad changes, and CI/CD - and remember Git is the local tool while GitHub/GitLab are optional hosts built on top of it.
